patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers away and received them
patterns.role_note: Australia → Fiji: Salesian Julian Fox; Melbourne → Samoa: Salesian priest (alleged); Melbourne → Israel (Malka Leifer flown out by her school); Fort Augustus → Australia: Denis Chrysostom Alexander; New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath; Kevin Lynch: Brisbane Grammar → St Paul's; Ballarat → Sydney: Fr Gerald Ridsdale.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Malka Leifer (Adass Israel School): first report 2008, first action 2021 (13 years). The school flew her to Israel in March 2008 before police were told; Israeli Deputy Health Minister Yaakov Litzman interfered with psychiatric assessments, later pleading guilty to breach of trust; extradition took six years from her 2014 arrest Gerald Ridsdale (Ballarat): first report 1975, first action 1993 (18 years). Bishop Mulkearns knew by 1975 and moved him through parishes; a police officer took the bishop's promise to handle it Frank Houston (Assemblies of God): first report 1999, first action 2015 (16 years). His son Brian Houston, then national president, and the national executive did not refer the 1999 allegations to police
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: Victoria 2015: Limitation period for child abuse civil claims removed (Feb 2015) New South Wales 2016: Limitation period removed (March 2016) Australian Capital Territory 2016: Limitation period removed (Aug 2016) Northern Territory 2017: Limitation period removed (June 2017) Tasmania 2017: Limitation period removed Western Australia 2018: Limitation period removed (April 2018) South Australia 2018: Limitation period removed (Sept 2018) Queensland 2018: Legislation amended (Nov 2018 per Shine); Queensland first removed the period for institutional child sexual abuse in 2016
patterns.pattern_summary: Most survivors disclose decades later, after the legal deadline to sue or prosecute has passed. Where legislatures tried to lift those deadlines, the institutions facing claims lobbied against it, and when the deadlines fell, many filed for bankruptcy. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million from 2014 to 2024. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1999: Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions (Forde Inquiry), 1999. Found abuse had occurred; 42 recommendations
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Malka Leifer: Extradited January 2021; convicted 3 April 2023; Litzman took a plea deal for breach of trust and resigned from the Knesset (2022)
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into Australia on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans (receiving or involved). Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008). Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1994: Crimes (Child Sex Tourism) Amendment Act 1994 in force 5 July 1994 — one of the first offender-country laws 2017: Australia: laws from 13 Dec 2017 allow cancelling passports of up to 20,000 registered child sex offenders; about 800 registered offenders had travelled abroad the previous year
patterns.pattern_summary: Child sex tourism followed enforcement around the map. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed Ermita in 1992, businesses moved to Angeles City. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Police ran abuse sites to catch users
patterns.role_note: Queensland Police Task Force Argos ran the Childs Play site for about 11 months (2016–17).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role_note: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013; Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008); Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report; Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7; Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry; Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions; Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia; Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale); Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care; Brisbane Grammar / St Paul's — counsellor abuse; Governor-General resigns over church handling; Royal Commission Case Study 36 — Church of England Boys' Society; Dio.

cases.title: Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Ballarat; Bishop Ronald Mulkearns
cases.what: Gerald Ridsdale, ordained 1961, was convicted in a series of trials from 1993 of abusing more than 70 children; he died in prison in 2025. He was moved between parishes including Mildura, Swan Hill, Warrnambool, Apollo Bay, Edenhope and Mortlake, then to Sydney. The Royal Commission's Ballarat report of 6 December 2017 found Bishop Mulkearns knew of his offending by late 1975 and still reappointed him, a 'catastrophic' failure. It also found police obstruction of a 1972 investigation of Monsignor John Day.
cases.cover_up: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

cases.title: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
cases.who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cases.what: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.
cases.cover_up: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.

cases.title: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane — Archbishop Peter Hollingworth's handling of abuse
cases.who: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane; Toowoomba Preparatory School; Church of England Boys' Society
cases.what: Peter Hollingworth was Anglican Archbishop of Brisbane from 1989 to 2001 and became Governor-General in June 2001. In December 2001 he faced allegations that he had handled sexual abuse cases poorly as archbishop. His successor, Phillip Aspinall, set up a church inquiry in February 2002 into the handling of nine abuse cases; its report was tabled in the Queensland Parliament on 1 May 2003, and Aspinall said Hollingworth had made a 'grave and serious' error of judgement. Hollingworth announced his resignation as Governor-General on 25 May 2003.
cases.cover_up: A diocesan inquiry found that in 1993 Archbishop Hollingworth allowed a known paedophile to keep working as a priest. He later became Governor-General of Australia.

cases.title: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
cases.who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
cases.what: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, and the order's later Hebron Trust were described by survivors to the Royal Commission as 'hell on earth'. Its August 2023 report found widespread sexual and physical abuse: more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended Marylands reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served at Marylands and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. At Hebron Trust youths were abused by Brother Bernard McGrath, who has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.
cases.cover_up: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements

cases.title: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
cases.who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
cases.what: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.
cases.cover_up: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.

cases.title: Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care
cases.who: Tasmanian Government: Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital paediatric ward, public schools, Child Safety Services, Tasmania Police
cases.what: The commission, called in 2020 after a podcast aired allegations against Launceston General Hospital paediatric nurse James Griffin (who died in 2019 after being charged with child sexual offences), released a 3,500-page final report in 2023 with 75 findings and 191 recommendations. It found the state's response to child sexual abuse since 2000 had too often been inadequate, sometimes to protect reputations. Children at Ashley Youth Detention Centre had experienced systematic harm and abuse for decades and sexual abuse remained a 'live and current' risk; the commission repeated its call for Ashley to close. Premier Jeremy Rockliff apologised in parliament.
cases.cover_up: Launceston General Hospital failed to act on a 2011 or 2012 disclosure about nurse James Griffin, leaving children at risk for eight years; Tasmania Police failed to act on 'highly probative' evidence from the Australian Federal Police in 2015; the government had been on notice about unlawful isolation at Ashley since at least 2013.

cases.title: Royal Commission — Catholic Church data, Australia
cases.who: Catholic Church in Australia, incl. St John of God Brothers (40.4% of brothers accused)
cases.what: Data presented to the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse on 6 February 2017 showed 4,444 people reported abuse to Catholic authorities between 1980 and 2015, at more than 1,000 institutions, naming 1,880 alleged perpetrators. About 7% of priests who served between 1950 and 2010 were alleged perpetrators; 40.4% of St John of God Brothers were accused. Religious brothers (32%) and priests (30%) were the largest groups. The commission referred 309 cases to police.

cases.title: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
cases.who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cases.what: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.
cases.cover_up: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Australia — forced adoptions: Senate inquiry 2012 and national apology 2013
cases.who: Australian governments, hospitals, churches and adoption agencies
cases.what: From the late 1950s to the 1970s tens of thousands of babies of unmarried, mostly teenage mothers were taken for adoption, often without informed consent. A Senate Community Affairs References Committee report in February 2012 ('Commonwealth Contribution to Former Forced Adoption Policies and Practices') urged a national apology. Prime Minister Julia Gillard delivered it on 21 March 2013. Several state and territory parliaments had apologised before this, starting with Western Australia in 2010.

cases.title: Australia — Stolen Generations: Bringing Them Home (1997) and national apology (2008)
cases.who: Australian federal, state and territory governments; church and state missions and institutions
cases.what: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were forcibly removed from their families under government policies roughly between 1910 and 1970 and placed in institutions, missions, foster or adoptive families. The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission's 1997 report 'Bringing Them Home' estimated that between one in three and one in ten Indigenous children were forcibly removed in that period, and recommended a national apology; Prime Minister John Howard refused, and Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised on 13 February 2008. Redress schemes followed, including Tasmania (2006) and NSW (2017), and in August 2021 a A$378 million Commonwealth scheme paying A$75,000 to each eligible survivor removed in the Northern Territory, the ACT or the Jervis Bay Territory (about 3,600 people).

cases.title: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
cases.who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
cases.what: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.

cases.title: South Korea — Brothers Home children sent overseas for adoption
cases.who: Brothers Home (Busan detention facility); receiving agencies named by AP incl. Holt International, Children's Home Society of Minnesota
cases.what: Brothers Home was a state-backed facility where people deemed vagrants were confined and forced to work; the TRC recognised state culpability on 23 August 2022 and counted 657 deaths there 1975–1988. An AP investigation (November 2019) found Brothers Home organised the adoption of 19 children abroad in 1979–1986 and that six US agencies received children from it. In February 2025 the TRC confirmed at least 31 children were improperly sent overseas for adoption through the facility.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

flows.title: Seoul → Australia
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Australia; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Saigon → Australia (removal)
flows.what: Operation Babylift children sent to Australia.

flows.title: UK → Australia child migrants
flows.what: Children in British care were sent to institutions in Australia where IICSA found a catalogue of evidence of ill-treatment and sexual abuse; the last child was migrated in 1970.

flows.title: Kevin Lynch: Brisbane Grammar → St Paul's
flows.what: After complaints were quietly investigated at Brisbane Grammar in the early 1980s, counsellor Kevin Lynch later worked at St Paul's School, where he also abused students; he was charged in 1997.

flows.title: Australia → Philippines payments for livestreamed abuse
flows.what: AUSTRAC alleged Westpac failed to vet transactions that could be linked to child exploitation and live child sex shows in the Philippines (A$1.3bn penalty, 2020); an Australian man paid a Filipino mother while directing abuse over Skype for nearly five years. IJM's 2020 study ranked Australians third among purchasers.

flows.title: Australian offender relocates to the Philippines
flows.what: Peter Scully fled Melbourne for the Philippines in 2011 and ran a pay-per-view abuse site there; life sentence 2018.

flows.title: Australia → Philippines travelling offenders
flows.what: Several Australian men have been convicted in Australia for abusing children in the Philippines, including a flight attendant who abused 26 girls from 2010 to 2017.

flows.title: Australia → Southeast Asia registered offenders' travel
flows.what: Australia's Foreign Minister said about 800 registered child sex offenders travelled abroad in 2016, often to developing countries in Asia, with 40% not notifying police.

President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: India — Malaysian Social Services, Chennai: children kidnapped for adoption
cases.who: Malaysian Social Services adoption agency
cases.what: Police suspected the family running the Malaysian Social Services agency since 1991 of kidnapping and trafficking more than 350 children; in May 2005 Chennai police arrested three family members and six others. Children allegedly had their appearance changed and histories fabricated; officers found files for 120 children sent overseas. TIME reported in 2008 that Australian authorities had earlier warnings.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
cases.who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cases.what: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.
cases.cover_up: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

cases.title: Operation Atlantic — FBI and EU follow-up to Boylover network
cases.who: Online offender networks incl. members of the Boylover network
cases.what: A joint FBI–EU investigation coordinated by Europol from November 2010. By February 2012, 37 child sex offenders had been identified and 17 arrested for molestation and production of illegal content; 8 victims were identified. Two targets had been members of the Boylover network tackled in Operation Rescue.

cases.title: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
cases.who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
cases.what: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

flows.title: Seoul → Netherlands
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Netherlands; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Colombo → Netherlands
flows.what: Sri Lankan babies adopted to the Netherlands in the 1980s, many through baby farms and falsified papers; others went to the UK, Sweden, Denmark and Germany.

flows.title: Athens → Netherlands
flows.what: Greek-born children adopted to Netherlands 1950–1975; Greece restored their citizenship by law on 2 May 2025.

flows.title: Buyers in 24 countries → Philippines (HSI data)
flows.what: Europol's 2024 sprint on US HSI data: chats between about 12,000 criminal customer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines; packages may lead 24 countries to 197 buyers. Origin point is The Hague (sprint host), not a buyer country.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in the Netherlands (IWF 2025)
flows.what: The Netherlands was the largest host of IWF-actioned material for years (47% in 2018); its share fell to 11% in 2025. INHOPE 2025 still ranks it first for confirmed CSAM (36%).

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: 2000: Statute of Limitations (Amendment) Act 2000 (passed 21 June 2000) gave a one-year window to bring claims for sexual abuse suffered as a minor and introduced a disability-based extension
patterns.pattern_summary: Most survivors disclose decades later, after the legal deadline to sue or prosecute has passed. Where legislatures tried to lift those deadlines, the institutions facing claims lobbied against it, and when the deadlines fell, many filed for bankruptcy. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million from 2014 to 2024. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 1999: Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse (Laffoy, then Ryan Commission), 1999-2009. Ryan Report 20 May 2009: sexual abuse endemic in boys' institutions; religious authorities shielded orders amid a "culture of self-serving secrecy"; state inspectors failed to stop it
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Holy See and the Murphy Commission (Ireland): No Vatican files supplied
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2018: scandal: Tusla refers 126 illegal birth registrations by St Patrick's Guild (May)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role: Welfare state, church and unmarried mothers
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2017: Ireland: Criminal Law (Sexual Offences) Act 2017 gives worldwide jurisdiction over Irish offenders
patterns.pattern_summary: Child sex tourism followed enforcement around the map. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed Ermita in 1992, businesses moved to Angeles City. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad; Ryan Commission — state-funded industrial schools and reformatories, Ireland; Mother and Baby Homes Commission — Ireland; Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns; Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin; Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady
cases.who: Diocese of Stockton; Bishop Roger Mahony (later Cardinal Archbishop of Los Angeles)
cases.what: Irish-born priest Oliver O'Grady, ordained in 1971 for the Diocese of Stockton, abused children from about 1973 and was moved between parishes. Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns by 1980 and moved him in 1984. O'Grady was convicted in 1993 and sentenced to 14 years; a 1998 civil jury awarded $30 million (reduced to $7 million). Paroled and deported to Ireland in 2000, he was convicted there for child abuse images in 2012 and 2020.
cases.cover_up: After police declined to charge him in 1984, Bishop Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor; Mahony said he was unaware of molestation reports, although a letter about earlier abuse was in O'Grady's personnel file.

cases.title: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020)
cases.who: Romanian organized criminal group using the 'loverboy' method
cases.what: On 9 September 2020 a Romanian–UK Joint Investigation Team supported by Eurojust arrested 21 members of a hierarchical group active since 2009 that seduced vulnerable Romanian girls with false promises of relationships, exploited minors in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18, and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. Thirty-two house searches were carried out (23 in Romania, 9 in the UK). Eurojust said Romania and the UK had cooperated in 76 trafficking investigations in four years.

cases.title: Fr Brendan Smyth — Norbertine order
cases.who: Norbertine order (Kilnacrott Abbey); Fr Brendan Smyth
cases.what: Norbertine priest Brendan Smyth abused children for decades from the 1950s in Northern Ireland, the Republic and the United States; the BBC put the number at at least 143. In 1975 Seán Brady, later Cardinal, attended church meetings where two teenage victims were sworn to secrecy; their evidence was never given to police. The Irish government's delay in acting on the RUC's extradition request led to the collapse of the Reynolds coalition in 1994. He was jailed in Northern Ireland in 1994 for abusing dozens of children there, and in July 1997 was sentenced in Dublin to 12 years for abusing 20 children in the Republic. He died in the Curragh Prison in August 1997. The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry (2017) found the Norbertine order moved him to another diocese despite knowing his history.
cases.cover_up: Norbertines moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries without reporting him; at a 1975 church inquiry two boys signed oaths of silence; mishandled extradition by the Irish Attorney General's office contributed to the fall of the government in 1994

cases.title: Ryan Commission — industrial schools run by religious orders
cases.who: Christian Brothers (most boys' institutions), Sisters of Mercy (most girls' institutions) and other Catholic orders
cases.what: The Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse reported on 20 May 2009 after a nine-year investigation of more than 250 church-run institutions that held over 30,000 children from the 1930s to the 1990s. It found sexual abuse 'endemic' in boys' institutions run mainly by the Christian Brothers; the Sisters of Mercy ran most girls' institutions. The 2,600-page report names no perpetrators after a Christian Brothers lawsuit. A parallel state redress scheme paid about 12,000 people an average of €65,000.
cases.cover_up: Christian Brothers sued the commission in 2004 to keep members' names out; no real names of perpetrators published; findings not to be used for prosecutions; state Department of Education inspections failed

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Ireland — Mother and Baby Homes Commission: 9,000 child deaths; adoptions abroad
cases.who: Religious orders (incl. Bon Secours Sisters), local authorities and the Irish state
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation's final report, published on 12 January 2021, covered 14 mother and baby homes and 4 county homes. About 56,000 women and 57,000 children were placed or born in them between 1922 and 1998. About 9,000 children died there, about 15% of all the children in the institutions, with infant mortality about double the national average. The homes doubled as orphanages and adoption agencies, and women faced pressure to place their children for adoption; Ireland did not legislate for adoption until 1952. On 13 January 2021 Taoiseach Micheál Martin apologised for 'the profound generational wrong visited upon Irish mothers and their children'. (The care agent may hold the home-conditions record; this record focuses on removals and adoptions.)
cases.cover_up: In May 2018 Tusla referred 126 cases of births falsely registered by the St Patrick's Guild adoption agency (illegal registrations that hid children's identities).

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Murphy Report — Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin
cases.what: The Commission of Investigation into the Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin reported on 26 November 2009. It examined a representative sample of 46 priests out of 102 within its remit; 320 people complained of child sexual abuse between 1975 and 2004. It found former Archbishops McQuaid, Ryan, McNamara and Connell failed to report what they knew to the Gardaí, and said the archdiocese's move to take out insurance against abuse claims showed it knew abuse was a potential major cost. It also criticised the Gardaí for treating priests as outside their remit; the Garda Commissioner called the report 'difficult and disturbing reading'.
cases.cover_up: Abuse 'covered up' 1975–2004; bishops generally did not report to Gardaí before 1996; archdiocese took out insurance against abuse litigation from 1987; Gardaí knew of complaints against Fr Tony Walsh in 1990–91 and took no action

cases.title: Ferns Report — Diocese of Ferns
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Ferns
cases.what: The state Ferns Inquiry, published 25 October 2005, examined more than 100 allegations of child sexual abuse made between 1962 and 2002 against 21 priests of the diocese. Bishop Donal Herlihy moved accused priests temporarily and then reinstated them, and ordained men he knew or should have known posed a risk. Bishop Brendan Comiskey never got a priest to stand aside from ministry. The report found Garda handling of one of eight formal complaints 'wholly inadequate' and some pre-1988 complaints were not recorded.
cases.cover_up: Bishop Herlihy moved accused priests to other posts or dioceses for a period, then reinstated them; Gardaí failed to record or properly investigate some pre-1988 complaints

cases.title: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
cases.who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cases.what: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.
cases.cover_up: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

flows.title: Ireland → United States: Fr Brendan Smyth
flows.what: The Norbertine order knew of Smyth's abuse and moved him between parishes, dioceses and countries, including assignments in the US, sometimes without warning bishops; he abused at least 143 children.

patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 5,797 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

patterns.role_note: Russia — Dima Yakovlev Law bans adoption by US citizens; Russia — 'Abandoned by the State': violence and neglect in orphanages for children with disabilities.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Russia — Dima Yakovlev Law bans adoption by US citizens
cases.who: Russian state
cases.what: On 28 December 2012 President Putin signed a law banning the adoption of Russian children by US families, effective 1 January 2013. It was named after Dima Yakovlev, a Russian toddler adopted by Americans who died in 2008 after being left for hours in a hot car; his adoptive father was found not guilty of involuntary manslaughter. The law was widely seen as retaliation for the US Magnitsky Act, signed on 14 December 2012. In 2010 a US adoptive mother had sent her 7-year-old adopted son alone on a one-way flight back to Russia, causing outrage. (This is a closure event, not a trafficking finding.)

cases.title: Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families
cases.who: Russian state; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree easing Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families; Russia created a register of families wishing to adopt Ukrainian children and paid families per adopted child granted citizenship. Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. On 17 March 2023 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL (14 February 2023) documented a 'systematic' programme of re-education and adoption. (Deportations and camps are recorded by the conflict agent; this record covers the adoption element.)

cases.title: Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
cases.who: Russian state: President Vladimir Putin; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022. The UN Commission of Inquiry found a transfer of 31 children in May 2022 was unlawful deportation and a war crime; Lvova-Belova's own bulletin said 380 orphans had been placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children from institutions transferred in February 2022. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for 're-education'.

cases.title: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
cases.who: Telegram (messaging platform)
cases.what: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram was not a member of NCMEC or the IWF and had ignored repeated requests to join. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

cases.title: Blue Orchid — Russian site selling abuse videos
cases.who: Blue Orchid website
cases.what: A Moscow-based website that sold videotapes of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly mailed to customers in the United States. The investigation began in May 2000 when Moscow police asked the US Customs Service for help; Russian police arrested the alleged operators in December 2000 and the site was shut in January 2001. By 26 March 2001 US Customs announced that four US citizens and five Russians had been arrested, with customers arrested in California, New York and Indiana and leads passed to Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands.

cases.title: Russia — 'Abandoned by the State': violence and neglect in orphanages for children with disabilities
cases.who: Russian state orphanages for children with disabilities
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 15 September 2014, based on more than 200 interviews and visits to 10 state orphanages, found that many children with disabilities suffered serious abuse and neglect by staff, including beatings, sedative injections and being sent to psychiatric hospitals as punishment. Children deemed most severely disabled were confined to cribs in 'lying-down rooms', often tied to furniture. The report did not centre on sexual abuse; it is recorded here as institutional abuse and removal of children from families.
cases.cover_up: Children had few if any meaningful ways to seek help or report abuse; health workers pressured parents to give up disabled children.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Ukraine — rape and sexual violence by Russian forces incl. children (UN Commission of Inquiry)
cases.who: Russian armed forces and authorities
cases.what: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed the war crimes of rape and other sexual violence; cases it investigated included a 16-year-old girl, and in September 2022 it said it had documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General.

cases.title: Ukraine — UN-verified abduction of children by Russian armed forces and authorities (2022–2023)
cases.who: Russian armed forces, affiliated armed groups and Russian authorities in occupied territories
cases.what: The UN Secretary-General verified the abduction, beginning in 2022 and continuing into 2023, of 122 children (75 boys, 47 girls) attributed to Russian armed forces, affiliated armed groups and Russian authorities in occupied Ukrainian territories; 91 abductions by Russian armed forces had been verified for 2022. The 2025 report welcomed the reunification of two of these children and said the whereabouts of the rest remained unknown.

patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 1996: Cambodia: 1996 Law on Suppression of the Kidnapping, Trafficking and Exploitation of Human Persons 2002: Svay Pak (Phnom Penh): child prostitution "bustling", driven by Western child-sex tourism after child prostitution in Thailand was cracked down upon 2003: 22 January 2003 police raid on Svay Pak child brothels — widely advertised in advance; no arrests; nearly all children moved beforehand to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. A Dateline NBC–IJM operation later in 2003 rescued 37 girls 2005: Cambodian government shut down Svay Pak brothels (2005); by 2006 prostitutes "no longer operate[d] with impunity"; 2008 Dateline: brothels "moved out of town"; 2011 CNN: trade had gone underground 2008: Cambodia: Law on Suppression of Human Trafficking and Sexual Exploitation (2008)

cases.title: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
cases.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
cases.what: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. Facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions for US families in 1997–2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

cases.title: Michael Pepe — former US Marine jailed 210 years for abusing girls in Cambodia
cases.who: Michael Joseph Pepe (retired US Marine Corps captain)
cases.what: Pepe travelled to Cambodia in 2005, was arrested there in 2006 and charged in the US in 2007. His first conviction was overturned by the Ninth Circuit in 2018; at a retrial in August 2021 victims testified he drugged, bound, beat and raped them, and prosecutors showed homemade abuse material. On 14 February 2022 a Los Angeles federal judge sentenced him to 210 years. The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the Cambodian National Police.

cases.title: Ronald Boyajian — 70 years for buying a 9-year-old girl in Svay Pak
cases.who: Ronald Gerard Boyajian (US registered sex offender)
cases.what: Boyajian, a registered sex offender with 1995 California convictions, was arrested in Cambodia in February 2009 on what prosecutors called his 35th trip to Asia over nine years, and was among the first three men expelled to the US under ICE's 'Operation Twisted Traveler' in August 2009. Convicted of illicit sexual conduct with a nine-year-old girl in Svay Pak, he was sentenced on 1 August 2016 to 70 years and ordered to pay $40,000 restitution.

cases.title: Operation Twisted Traveler — ICE crackdown on US offenders in Cambodia (2009)
cases.who: US Immigration and Customs Enforcement; Cambodian police
cases.what: In August 2009 three previously convicted US sex offenders arrested by Cambodian police in February — Ronald Boyajian, Erik Peeters and Jack Sporich — were returned to Los Angeles as the first defendants charged under 'Operation Twisted Traveler'. ICE head John Morton called Cambodia 'ground zero for child sex tourism'; ICE had stationed an agent in Cambodia full-time. Peeters was accused of abusing at least three Cambodian boys and Sporich of abusing a boy in Siem Reap (accusations at the time).

cases.title: Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline
cases.who: Brothels in Svay Pak (mostly ethnic Vietnamese victims)
cases.what: Svay Pak, a poor fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became notorious as a place where foreign men bought sex with children; CNN in 2017 reported girls there being sold by their families. After crackdowns by the government, police and international agencies, open street sales ended and the trade moved to more hidden venues such as massage parlours and karaoke bars. ABC News reported in 2017 that survey estimates of the share of minors among Cambodia's sex workers had fallen from nearly 35% to 1–2%.
cases.cover_up: The 22 January 2003 police raid was widely advertised in advance; almost all children had been moved and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had extorted brothel owners.

cases.title: Cambodia — child sex tourism and brothels; scam compounds (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Brothel and entertainment operators; foreign and Cambodian offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Cambodian men and men from Australia, South Africa, the United States and other countries in Asia and Europe sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, increasingly via social media; children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts; and women and girls are exploited in online scam compounds.
cases.cover_up: The report says official complicity, including at senior levels, inhibited effective law enforcement.

cases.title: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
cases.who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
cases.what: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.

cases.title: Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations
cases.who: Private residential care institutions ('orphanages') in Cambodia
cases.what: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states: 'Some Cambodian orphanages purchase local children from economically disadvantaged families and subject them to malnutrition and unclean living conditions in their facilities for the purpose of attracting and profiting from charitable donations; some of these children are at further risk of sex trafficking and domestic servitude as a result of poor government oversight of adoption processes.' The same report links orphanages and trafficking in Nepal, Nigeria, Haiti, Sri Lanka and Moldova.
cases.cover_up: The report states 'endemic corruption aids and abets trafficking crimes'.

flows.what: Most children in Svay Pak brothels were ethnic Vietnamese, many sold by destitute families; US TIP 2025 still reports ethnic Vietnamese women and girls exploited in Cambodian cities and tourist areas.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Dominican Republic → Poland: Fr Wojciech Gil.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2019: State Commission for investigating sexual abuse of children under 15 (Państwowa Komisja ds. Pedofilii), Act of 30 Aug 2019, full membership sworn 24 July 2020. Criticised in Aug 2022 that church documents sent to the Vatican were out of its reach and church files are destroyed ten years after conviction under canon law
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Fr Wojciech Gil (accused with Wesołowski) (2013): Arrested in Poland 17 Feb 2014; convicted in Poland (seven years, per NCR citation)
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

cases.title: Poland — bishops' 2019 figures, Sekielski films and sanctions on bishops
cases.who: Polish Episcopal Conference; Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź; Bishop Edward Janiak; Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz
cases.what: In March 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference released a study reporting 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The Sekielski brothers' documentaries 'Tell No One' (May 2019, over 23 million YouTube views) and 'Hide and Seek' (May 2020) led to Vatican investigations of bishops under Vos estis lux mundi. In June 2020 Pope Francis put the Diocese of Kalisz under an apostolic administrator and on 17 October 2020 accepted the resignation of Bishop Edward Janiak, accused in 'Hide and Seek' of failing to act against an accused priest. Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź was also investigated, and on 6 November 2020 the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz, who died ten days later.
cases.cover_up: Bishops sanctioned by the Vatican for protecting abusers: Janiak (Kalisz) ordered to resign June 2020; Głódź (Gdańsk) removed August 2020 after covering up abuse by Henryk Jankowski and Franciszek Cybula

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
cases.cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
cases.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cases.what: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
cases.cover_up: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.
